idiom_name: function memoize<K extends Key, V>(fn: (key: K) => V): (key: K) => V
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the key contract to the JavaScript map idiom: constrain K to a key type the runtime can actually distinguish - primitives or tuples of primitives - because the type system cannot express structural key equality for the Map (two structurally equal objects are two entries). Hashing arguments behind an interface (a keyOf/serialize function passed to the wrapper) moves the decision to the boundary where the types still line up. Map, WeakMap and their generics require the ES2015 library in the compiler configuration, so a project targeting an older lib silently loses the types and must fall back to index signatures; that configuration detail is the difference between a memoized map wrapper and an object-shaped cache with prototype-key hazards.
pitfalls: The key type is a promise the compiler cannot keep: structurally equal objects are distinct Map keys, so type the wrapper on primitives or tuples and serialise at the boundary.
Object-shaped caches (Record<string, V>) inherit prototype keys and numeric-key coercion; Map avoids both, which matters when keys come from user input.
A generic wrapper loses the original function's parameter list unless the key type mirrors it, so multi-argument functions either take one key or need a keyOf function.
Every result handed out is the same object: TypeScript's readonly types do not stop runtime mutation of cached values by callers.

variants.name: WeakMap keyed by instance for per-object derivations
variants.implementation_notes: For per-instance derived data the WeakMap form is both the memory-safe and the type-safe choice: the key type is object (or a concrete class type), the value type is the derivation, and entries disappear with their key instead of pinning the instance forever, which is the classic memo leak that shows up as objects never being collected. It is the standard fix for caching method results per instance: rather than decorating the method and capturing this in the key, key the cache by the instance itself. The documented limits are the price: keys must be objects, and the store is not enumerable, so it cannot report size or support eviction policies - use a Map when the cache must be observable or bounded.
pitfalls: WeakMap keys must be objects, so primitive-keyed memoization (ids, slugs) needs a Map or a two-level structure.
No size, no iteration, no clear: an eviction policy or cache metrics cannot be built on it.
Entries vanish silently with their keys, so a caller that keeps only the value observes recomputation.
Concurrent async interleavings can still compute the same key twice; neither WeakMap nor Map offers an atomic compute-if-absent.

variants.name: React useMemo for render-scoped derivations (framework)
variants.idiom_name: useMemo(compute, deps) / React Compiler automatic memoization
variants.implementation_notes: Inside a React component the framework owns the cache: useMemo caches a calculation between re-renders until its dependencies change, comparing them with Object.is, and React's own documentation is explicit about the contract - rely on it only as a performance optimization, because the cache may be discarded (for example when the component suspends) and in development Strict Mode calls the calculation twice to surface impurity. The migration path is the React Compiler, which memoizes automatically and reduces the need for manual calls. That makes this variant structurally different from an application-level memo: the value is render-scoped, not process-scoped, and correctness must never depend on the hit.
pitfalls: The cache is a performance optimisation, not a semantic guarantee: React may throw it away and dev Strict Mode runs the calculation twice, so nothing observable may depend on the hit.
A dependency that is a new reference on every render (an inline object or array) breaks memoization entirely; the dependency list must be stable.
The hook must be called at the top level of a component or hook, never in loops or conditions, which rules it out for data-dependent caching.
Memoizing inside a component caches per component instance and per render tree position - it does not share results across instances or requests.
